key_terms.meaning: Software that turns human text or speech into structure a computer can act on: tags, trees, vectors, decisions.
A fixed, documented collection of real text used to train models and compare results across papers.
One unit produced by tokenization: a word, a punctuation mark, a number or an emoji.
Any decision that rewrites raw text into a standard form before tokens are cut, such as lowercasing or expanding contractions.
A compact pattern built from literals and operators such as * + | ? and brackets that denotes a set of strings.
A machine of states and labelled transitions that reads a string once, left to right, and accepts or rejects it.
Chopping word endings with fixed rules; the result need not be a real word (studies → studi).
Reducing a word to its dictionary base form, the lemma, using morphological analysis (was → be).
A very frequent token such as the, is, of that is dropped because it carries little topic information.
The smallest unit of a word that carries meaning or grammatical function.
A morpheme that can stand alone as a word, like book.
A morpheme that must attach to another, like the -s in books.
Adding a suffix to mark number, tense or case without changing the word's part of speech (book → books).
Adding an affix that changes meaning or part of speech (nation → national → nationalise).
A language type in which words are long chains of clearly separable morphemes, one meaning per morpheme.
A finite-state machine with two tapes that maps a surface word to lemma plus features, and back.
The lowest total cost of single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions that turns one string into another.
Minimum edit distance where every insertion, deletion and substitution costs 1.
A misspelling that is itself a valid word, so a dictionary lookup cannot catch it (form for from).
The layer of meaning that depends on speaker intent and context, as in sarcasm or an indirect request.

takeaways: NLP has moved from hand-written rules, to counts over corpora, to learned representations, and each stage still solves problems the others handle badly.
Language is analysed in layers — phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics, discourse — and each layer brings its own kind of ambiguity.
A regular expression denotes a set of strings, and every such set has an equivalent finite-state automaton that decides membership in one pass.
Tokenization and normalization are decided together: change the casing or the punctuation rule and the token list changes.
Stemming is fast and crude, lemmatization is slower and correct; stop-word removal helps retrieval but can destroy negation and sentiment.
A finite-state transducer compiles morphological rules into a two-tape machine that analyses a word and generates it back, both from the same rule set.
Minimum edit distance is the cheapest sequence of single-character edits; it underlies spelling correction, word alignment and fuzzy matching.
A corpus is only useful if it is fixed, cleaned and documented, so every later model is trained and compared on the same data.
bank_note: Long answers here are judged on three things: a clear definition, a worked example (an automaton, a transducer, an edit-distance table) and an honest statement of where the method fails.

bank.q: Define natural language processing and trace its evolution from rule-based systems, through statistical methods, to learned representations. Give one task where each approach still wins.
outline: Definition of NLP as mapping text to structure a machine can act on
Rule-based era: hand-written grammars and pattern rules; strengths on narrow, well-specified domains
Statistical era: counts from corpora, n-grams, HMMs; strengths on noisy real text
Neural era: embeddings, RNNs, transformers, pretraining on large unlabelled text
One concrete task per era with the reason it suits that method

bank.q: Explain the levels of language analysis — phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics and discourse — with the unit each one works on and one ambiguity that arises at each level.
outline: Each level named with its unit: sound, sound pattern, morpheme, sentence structure, literal meaning, intended meaning, connected text
A concrete example of ambiguity at each level
Why NLP pipelines are built layer by layer and where errors propagate
Note that higher layers need lower layers as input

bank.q: What is a regular expression? Explain the operators used to build one and show, with a diagram, how any regular expression can be converted to an equivalent finite-state automaton.
outline: Regular expression defined as a pattern denoting a set of strings
The operators: concatenation, union, Kleene star, plus, optional, wildcard, character classes, anchors
Definition of a finite-state automaton: states, transitions, start state, accept states
Thompson-style construction: base cases for a single symbol and epsilon, then union, concatenation and star by combining automata
Why the resulting machine reads the string once and runs in linear time

bank.q: Explain tokenization and text normalization as a chain of decisions, and show why different decisions give different token lists for the same sentence.
outline: Tokenization as segmenting a character stream into the units later stages count
Ambiguous cases: clitics (can't), hyphens, decimal points, abbreviations, URLs, emoji, hashtags
Normalization choices: case folding, Unicode normalization, whitespace, punctuation handling, contraction expansion
Same sentence, two token lists, with the trade-off stated
Rule-based, regex-based and subword tokenizers compared briefly

bank.q: Compare stemming and lemmatization. Give three word examples each and state when stop-word removal harms an application.
outline: Stemming: fixed suffix-stripping rules, e.g. Porter; output may not be a word
Lemmatization: needs a lexicon and part-of-speech, returns the dictionary base form
Worked examples: studies/studi, was/be, better/good
Stemming is faster and recall-oriented; lemmatization is slower and precision-oriented
Stop-word removal harms negation handling, sentiment analysis and phrase queries; name concrete cases like 'not good'

bank.q: Write a regular expression that matches Indian mobile numbers of the form 10 digits starting with 6, 7, 8 or 9, optionally written with +91 and spaces. Then draw the finite-state automaton for it and trace one accepted and one rejected string.
outline: Pattern with grouping, optional prefix and a character class for the first digit
Explanation of each operator used
Correct FSA with a state per position and a reject path
Trace of an accepted string such as +91 98765 43210
Trace of a rejected string and why it fails

bank.q: Using a dynamic-programming table, compute the minimum edit distance between the strings 'intent' and 'internet'. Show the backtrace and one cheapest edit script.
outline: Initialisation of the (m+1) × (n+1) table
Recurrence: insertion cost 1, deletion cost 1, substitution 0 if equal else 1, take the minimum
Correctly filled table, or a correct summary of every row
Backtrace path with the operations named in order
Final distance and edit script; note the transposition variant if used

bank.q: Design a full preprocessing pipeline for 50,000 scraped tweets about a Chennai power cut, covering cleaning, normalization, tokenization, stop words and lemmatization. Justify every step and say what you would keep that you might otherwise drop.
outline: Cleaning: HTML removal, URL and mention handling, emoji policy, deduplication
Normalization: Unicode, case folding, repeated characters, hashtag splitting
Tokenization choice suited to social text, not a whitespace split
Stop-word list choice, and keeping negations and sentiment-bearing words
Lemmatization or stemming choice with reason
Order of steps stated, plus an evaluation check on a small hand-labelled sample

bank.q: Build a finite-state transducer for English plural inflection and run it in both directions on 'box', 'boxes', 'city' and 'cities'.
outline: Lexical tape: lemma plus feature [+plural]; surface tape: the inflected word
Rules: add -s by default, -es after s, x, z, ch, sh, y to -ies after a consonant
Transducer drawn with arcs labelled lexical:surface
Generation trace for each word and analysis trace in reverse
Note that the same machine is inverted for analysis, and how irregular plurals escape it

bank.q: You must build a 5-million-word corpus on Indian government scheme announcements from the web. Describe your sources, scraping steps, cleaning, documentation and legal and ethical checks.
outline: Source list with formats: HTML, PDF, RSS
Scraping loop: fetch, respect robots.txt, rate limits, user agent, retries, caching
Extraction of main text, removal of navigation and boilerplate
Cleaning, deduplication, language identification, encoding normalization
Documentation: collection date, license, size, token count, known gaps
Ethics and law: terms of service, copyright, personal data, attribution

bank.q: Compare rule-based, statistical and neural approaches to NLP on data requirement, interpretability, handling of unseen input and cost. Recommend one approach for a low-resource Indian language and defend the choice.
outline: Each approach described by its mechanism, not its name
Comparison table across the four axes
Rule-based: little data, fully interpretable, brittle to variation
Statistical: needs annotated corpora, transparent probabilities, limited generalisation
Neural: needs large data or pretraining, opaque, strong generalisation
Recommendation for low-resource setting, e.g. rules or transducers plus cross-lingual transfer, with justification

bank.q: Evaluate minimum edit distance as a spelling corrector. Distinguish non-word from real-word errors, and explain why edit distance alone fails on the second kind.
outline: Non-word error detected by dictionary lookup; real-word error passes the lookup
Edit distance generates candidate corrections within a threshold
Ranking needs more than distance: frequency, context probability, keyboard cost
Why a real-word error needs an n-gram or contextual model
Cost of a wide threshold and how to bound it
Honest limit: transpositions, morphology, named entities, Indian language inflection

bank.q: Discuss morphological typology — isolating, agglutinative, fusional and compounding — and analyse how each type changes the design of an NLP system for an Indian language.
outline: Four types defined with one example language each, and the caveat that real languages mix types
Isolating: little morphology, tokenization is close to word segmentation
Agglutinative: long words, many suffixes, a transducer or FST lexicon pays off; rich vocabulary growth
Fusional: one suffix carries several features, harder analysis
Compounding: productive word formation, needs a compound handler
Consequences for stemming, lemmatization, vocabulary size, POS tagset design

bank.q: A team must choose stemming or lemmatization and a stop-word policy for a large document search system. Evaluate the options and justify a decision that balances precision and recall.
outline: Effect of conflation on index size and recall
Stemming: cheap, over-conflates (university/universe), hurts precision
Lemmatization: correct conflation, needs POS and a lexicon, slower
Stop-word removal: smaller index, faster queries, but breaks phrase queries and can drop meaning
Decision: lemmatization or light stemming plus a short, task-specific stop list
Measurement: precision and recall on a labelled query set

glossary.def: The field that builds systems which read, interpret or produce human language.
A fixed, documented body of real text used for training and evaluation.
One unit of text after segmentation, usually a word or punctuation mark.
A distinct token form; the number of types is the vocabulary size.
The step that cuts a character stream into tokens.
Rewriting raw text into a standard form before further processing.
A pattern that denotes a set of strings.
A five-tuple of states, alphabet, transitions, start state and accept states that accepts or rejects strings.
A finite-state machine that reads one tape and writes another, used for morphological analysis and generation.
A machine with exactly one transition per state and symbol, so its path is fixed.
The part of a word left after suffix stripping, not necessarily a word.
The dictionary base form under which inflected forms are listed.
A very frequent word dropped from an index or a model input.
The smallest meaningful unit of a word.
A bound morpheme attached to a root: prefix, suffix, infix or circumfix.
The core morpheme that carries the main meaning of a word.
Suffixation that adds grammatical features without changing word class.
Affixation that creates a new word, often of a different class.
Joining two or more free morphemes into one word.
A language whose words are long, regular chains of separately meaningful morphemes.
A language whose single suffix may encode several grammatical features at once.
A language with almost no inflection; grammatical information is carried by separate words.
The cheapest total cost of single-character edits that turns one string into another.
Swapping two adjacent characters, an edit operation in the Damerau variant.
A misspelling that is not a valid word, so a dictionary check finds it.
